papers.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767524 v1

summary.one_liner: Proximity-labeling screen under ciliogenesis-restrictive versus permissive conditions identifies SAMD4B, a centrosome-associated protein, as required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish, possibly via ciliary recruitment of ARL13B and SMO.
summary.plain: Cells build tiny antenna-like structures called primary cilia that help them receive developmental signals, including the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signal that guides how embryos form. This study used a labeling method that tags proteins near each other to find new factors involved in building or using these cilia. It found that a protein called SAMD4B, which sits near the cell's central organizing structure (the centrosome), is needed for Shh signaling in mouse cells and for normal eye development in zebrafish.
summary.why: Cilia defects are linked to many developmental disorders, so new regulators of Shh signaling are of interest. The paper suggests a link between SAMD4B, previously known for RNA condensates in the cytoplasm, and ciliary signaling; the text does not establish how general this role is or whether it matters in human disease.
summary.background:
- Primary cilia: small hair-like projections on cells that act as signal-receiving hubs.
- Sonic hedgehog (Shh): a signaling pathway essential for embryo development and tissue maintenance.
- Centrosome: a cell structure that organizes microtubules (cell's internal scaffolding) and anchors cilia formation.
- ARL13B and SMO: proteins that must move into the cilium for Shh signaling to work.
- Proximity labeling: a method that marks proteins lying close to a target protein so their interactions can be mapped.
- siRNA depletion: a way to switch off a gene temporarily to test its function.
- NIH3T3 cells (mouse cell line) and zebrafish are the model systems used.
- RNA condensates: droplet-like clusters of RNA and proteins inside the cell.

papers.abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

papers.title: Smyd1 regulates H3K4me3 to support adaptive fatty acid oxidation in the adult heart during lipid overload
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.763125 v1

summary.one_liner: In mice, high-fat diet transiently raises the histone methyltransferase Smyd1 and H3K4me3 in heart muscle cells, and cardiac Smyd1 heterozygous knockout worsens fatty acid oxidation gene responses, dysfunction and survival, with a Smyd1–PPARα interaction proposed as a mechanism.
summary.plain: Obesity can weaken the heart over time, partly because heart muscle cells stop burning fat efficiently. This study looked at a protein called Smyd1 that helps control gene activity, and found that in mice fed a high-fat diet it rises early on, which appears to help the heart keep burning fat. Mice with less Smyd1 in the heart did worse: their hearts weakened faster, enlarged, scarred more, and they were less likely to survive.
summary.why: It suggests a possible molecular route by which the heart adapts to fatty diets and where that adaptation could fail, which may matter for obesity-related heart disease. The findings are from mice, and the text does not show that the same mechanism operates in people or that targeting it would help.
summary.background:
- Fatty acid oxidation (FAO): the process by which cells break down fats to produce energy; the heart relies on it heavily.
- Obesity-related cardiomyopathy: weakening of the heart muscle linked to excess body fat.
- Histone methylation: chemical tags on the protein spools that DNA wraps around, which change how genes are switched on; H3K4me3 is one such tag linked to active genes.
- Smyd1: a histone methyltransferase, an enzyme that adds these tags, found mainly in muscle.
- PPARα: a nuclear receptor (a gene-switching protein) that turns on fat-burning genes.
- Co-immunoprecipitation: a lab method for testing whether two proteins physically bind together.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing: a method that measures gene activity in individual cells.
- Heterozygous knockout: a model where one of two working copies of a gene is removed.

papers.abstract: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are major risk factors for heart failure, and impaired fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is a key contributor to metabolic dysfunction in obesity-related cardiomyopathy. However, how the heart maintains FAO and adapts to chronic lipid overload remains poorly understood. Here, we identify SET and MYND domain-containing protein 1 (Smyd1), a muscle-specific histone methyltransferase, as an early compensatory regulator of cardiac metabolism in response to lipid overload. In wild-type mouse hearts, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding induced transient increases in Smyd1 expression and H3K4me3 levels during the early-to-mid phase of metabolic stress, both of which returned to baseline levels during prolonged HFD exposure. Single-cell RNA sequencing further revealed that this adaptive increase in Smyd1 expression occurred predominantly in cardiomyocytes. In contrast, cardiac-specific Smyd1 heterozygous knockout mice exhibited accelerated cardiac dysfunction, left ventricular dilation, increased myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival following HFD feeding. Mechanistically, Smyd1 deficiency impaired the adaptive upregulation of key FAO-related genes and reduced cardiac FAO activity. Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation analysis revealed an interaction between Smyd1 and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR), suggesting a potential mechanism by which Smyd1 supports FAO gene expression. Taken together, these findings identify Smyd1 as an early compensatory regulator that supports FAO-dependent metabolic adaptation and protects the heart against lipid overload-induced cardiac dysfunction. This adaptive mechanism, involving H3K4me3 regulation and the Smyd1-PPAR interaction, may provide potential therapeutic targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving cardiac metabolic flexibility in obesity-related cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767488 v1

summary.background:
- Adipocytes are fat-storing cells; SGBS is a human pre-adipocyte line that matures into fat cells in the lab.
- Palmitic acid (PA) is a long-chain saturated fatty acid common in the diet; BSA (bovine serum albumin) is the carrier protein used for the control condition.
- Insulin signalling works through proteins such as Akt and AS160; if it is impaired, cells take up less sugar, a feature of insulin resistance.
- NF-kB is an inflammation-related signalling pathway; MCP-1, IL-6 and IL-8 are inflammatory messenger molecules; adiponectin is a hormone usually considered protective.
- The secretome is the set of molecules a cell releases into its surroundings; it was tested by transferring it onto muscle cells (myotubes).
- The stromal vascular fraction (immune and support cells found in fat tissue) was absent here, which the authors note limits how far the results apply to real tissue.
summary.one_liner: In cultured SGBS human adipocytes, a 96-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure raised lipid droplet and cell size and shifted cytokine and adiponectin secretion, but did not impair insulin signalling in adipocytes or in co-cultured myotubes.
summary.plain:
Eating too much saturated fat is thought to help drive obesity and poor metabolic health, but it is unclear how much it damages human fat cells directly. This study grew fat cells from a human cell line (SGBS) in palmitic acid, a common saturated fat, for four days and checked their fat storage, inflammation signals, and the chemicals they released. The fat cells stored more fat and released more of some inflammatory signals, yet they did not become clearly dysfunctional, and their released chemicals did not block insulin action in muscle cells.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It suggests that a saturated fat alone, acting directly on fat cells without other immune or support cells present, may not be enough to produce the full set of problems linked to obesity. This is relevant to how fat tissue contributes to insulin resistance, though the result comes from a single cell model and says little about whole bodies.

papers.abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.

papers.title: Extra-sheath transplantation of human retinal organoids (hROs): effects on visual recovery and retinal repair following optic nerve injury
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767615 v1

summary.background:
- Retinal ganglion cells: the eye's output neurons whose long axons form the optic nerve to the brain.
- Optic nerve crush: a standard lab injury model that mechanically damages this nerve.
- Retinal organoids: three-dimensional tissue grown from stem cells that mimics parts of the retina.
- Microelectrode array (MEA): a plate that records electrical activity from cells.
- Electroretinography (ERG) and visual evoked potentials (VEP): recordings of electrical responses from the retina (ERG b-wave) and the visual cortex (VEP P2 peak) to light flashes.
- Optomotor response: a mouse's reflex to turn its head with rotating stripes, used to gauge vision.
- Immunostaining (RBPMS, TUJ1, IBA1): labelling that marks ganglion cells, their axons, and microglia (immune cells of the nervous system).
- Mouse strain C57: a common inbred laboratory mouse line.
summary.one_liner: In C57 mice with optic nerve crush, transplanting day-30 human retinal organoids at the injury site was associated with preserved optic-disc appearance, ganglion cell layer thickness, and flash VEP P2 amplitude, with a b-wave showing no between-group difference, though donor-derived circuit integration was not demonstrated.
summary.plain: Damage to the optic nerve, the cable that carries vision signals from the eye to the brain, can cause lasting vision loss. In this study, researchers placed small lab-grown human "mini-retinas" (retinal organoids) at the site of a crushed optic nerve in mice and tracked the eyes and visual responses for up to 28 days. Transplanted mice kept more of their nerve-cell layer and showed stronger visual-brain signals and better responses to moving stripes than mice with the crush alone, though the authors say the results do not yet prove the graft wired into the visual circuit.
summary.why: Optic nerve injury has few treatments that protect the nerve cells and restore signalling at the same time, so a graft-based approach is of interest. The text is measured about its limits: the benefits were incomplete compared with uninjured mice, and the behavioural light-dark test is non-specific, so the work is an early preclinical signal rather than evidence of a therapy.

papers.abstract: Traumatic optic nerve injury interrupts retinal ganglion cell output and can produce permanent visual disability, yet a therapeutic strategy that couples retinal protection with recovery of visual-pathway activity remains unavailable. Here, we evaluated human retinal organoid transplantation at the site of optic nerve crush in C57 mice. Human retinal organoids derived from embryonic stem cells were used at day 30 and showed retinal-lineage immunoreactivity together with spontaneous microelectrode-array activity. Across post-surgical days 7, 14, and 28, transplantation was associated with preservation of optic-disc appearance and ganglion cell layer thickness. The structural benefit became statistically distinguishable from the crush group at day 28 and remained incomplete relative to the uninjured or sham group. Serial RBPMS and TUJ1 immunostaining further supported attenuation of retinal ganglion cell body and neurite loss, while IBA1 staining indicated an altered microglial response. Full-field electroretinographic b-wave responses showed no detectable between-group differences, arguing against a major outer-retinal effect. In contrast, flash visual evoked potential P2 amplitude was higher in transplanted than in crush-only mice at all measured time points, consistent with improved visual-pathway responsiveness. Transplant recipients also showed enhanced optomotor responses across tested spatial-frequency and contrast conditions. Light-dark behavior shifted toward greater dark-compartment occupancy and activity, although this assay remains non-specific for visual recovery. Together, these findings support a model in which hROs transplantation at an optic nerve injury site promotes multi-level functional preservation after optic nerve crush. Definitive evidence for donor-derived circuit reconstruction will require graft tracing, synaptic validation, and prespecified electrophysiologic analyses.

papers.title: Endogenous activation of multiple stress-response pathways during meiosis promotes gamete fitness
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767631 v1

summary.background:
- Transcription factors: proteins that switch genes on or off; they are the control switches this paper studies.
- Meiosis: the cell division that produces haploid gametes (sperm, egg, or yeast spores) from diploid cells.
- Gametogenesis: the full process of making gametes, including meiosis and the packaging of gametes.
- Stress-response pathways: built-in cellular systems that respond to heat, oxidative damage and similar threats.
- Antioxidant genes (TSA1, AHP1): genes whose products help neutralize reactive oxygen molecules that can damage cells.
- Gamete fitness: how well a gamete survives and can contribute to the next generation; the text measures this only indirectly through yeast experiments.
- Budding yeast: a single-celled fungus widely used as a model organism in cell biology.
summary.one_liner: In budding yeast, four stress-responsive transcription factors (Hsf1, Skn7, Msn2 and Msn4) are active during gametogenesis without any added stress, and depleting Msn2, Msn4 and Skn7 together lowers gamete fitness, with the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1 identified as key targets.
summary.plain: When yeast cells make sex cells (gametes), they halve their chromosomes and reshape themselves in a major developmental process called meiosis. This paper asks whether the cell's built-in stress-defense switches also help that process succeed. The authors found that several of these switches turn on during meiosis even without any outside stress, and that turning off three of them at once makes the resulting gametes less fit. Two antioxidant genes, TSA1 and AHP1, appear to be the important downstream helpers.
summary.why: It suggests that the machinery cells use to cope with environmental damage is also part of normal development, not only an emergency response. This may matter for understanding how gametes stay healthy, though the text does not show how broadly the idea applies beyond yeast.

papers.abstract: Gametogenesis, the process of meiosis coupled to gamete formation, transforms diploid progenitor cells into haploid gametes through extensive cellular remodeling and rewiring of gene expression. Several stress-responsive transcription factors (TFs) are upregulated during gametogenesis, but whether the cellular mechanisms that handle environmental stress also support the success of this developmental process is largely unexplored. Here, we show that four stress-responsive TFs, Hsf1, Skn7, and the paralogs Msn2 and Msn4, are endogenously active during budding yeast gametogenesis in the absence of external stress and drive distinct gene expression programs. Simultaneous meiotic depletion of Msn2, Msn4, and Skn7 compromise the fitness of the resulting gametes. We identified just two TF-dependent targets, the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1, as important for gamete fitness, directly connecting TF activity to the protection of meiotic progeny. Our results demonstrate that the activation of canonical stress-response regulators is built into the meiotic program and suggest that such pathways can be repurposed during development to safeguard cellular health.

papers.title: Centimeter-sized Human Vitreous Organoids from Pluripotent Stem Cells
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767433 v1

summary.background:
- The vitreous is the transparent gel that fills the large chamber behind the lens of the eye.
- Organoids are small, three-dimensional tissue cultures grown from stem cells that mimic parts of an organ.
- Pluripotent stem cells can develop into many cell types; here they are human cells made to form eye-like tissue.
- Fibroblasts are connective-tissue cells that make structural proteins and scaffolding.
- TGF-beta is a signaling protein that directs cell growth and specialization.
- Transthyretin (TTR) is a protein that, when mutated, can misfold and build up as amyloid deposits; vitreous amyloidosis is a clouding of the vitreous caused by such deposits.
- Mouse development data were used as a comparison, per the text.
summary.one_liner: The authors identify a fibroblast-rich "growth edge" in human and mouse vitreous development and use TGF-beta signaling to differentiate human pluripotent stem cells into centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids that model a TTR-linked vitreous amyloidosis.
summary.plain: The vitreous is the clear, jelly-like filling of the eye that lets light reach the retina and helps keep the eye's pressure and shape stable. Scientists have not yet been able to rebuild it in the lab or repair it in the body. Here, the authors grew stem-cell-derived clumps of tissue that they call vitreous organoids, reaching about a centimeter in size, and report that they looked and behaved in ways similar to human vitreous.
summary.why: A lab model of the vitreous could help study how this tissue forms and how it fails, and may eventually inform repair strategies for eye diseases. The text reports that the organoids carried a disease-linked gene mutation and reproduced features of a patient condition, but whether this translates to treatment is not shown in the text, so its clinical reach remains uncertain.

papers.abstract: The vitreous, the largest intraocular tissue, provides a transparent light path and maintains the intraocular homeostasis. The reconstitution of the vitreous in vitro or in vivo remains an unsolved biomedical challenge. Here, we discovered a common feature, the "growth edge", constituted primarily of fibroblasts and their secreted proteins in human and mouse vitreous development. By leveraging the transforming growth factor beta signaling, we then generated centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids (VOs) through stepwise differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The VOs exhibited striking similarity to human vitreous in terms of physical transparency, vitreoretinal interface, molecular composition, biological profiles and regenerative transplantability. Lines of evidence supported that fibroblasts are the key cell hub for vitreous development. Finally, VOs with a transthyretin (TTR) mutation recapitulated the vitreous phenotypes of human patients with vitreous amyloidosis. Together, vitreous organoid technology opens avenues for future studies of human vitreous development, disease modeling, and regenerative therapeutics for a broad spectrum of human vitreoretinal diseases.

papers.title: Modelling Maternal-to-Zygotic Transition Dynamics to Identify Common Gene Expression Baselines in Zebrafish Development.
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767246 v1

summary.background:
- Maternal-to-zygotic transition: early embryos rely on RNA and proteins deposited by the mother until their own genome switches on (zygotic genome activation).
- RNA-seq: a method that counts how much of each gene's RNA is present in a sample, used here over a time course.
- ODE (ordinary differential equation) model: a set of equations describing how quantities such as RNA levels change over time, with parameters fitted to data.
- Clustering: sorting genes into groups with similar behaviour; fuzzy c-means allows a gene to partly belong to several groups.
- Poly(A) enrichment: a lab step that selects messenger RNA by its tail; it can bias which transcripts are measured.
- hpf: hours post fertilization, a standard embryo age unit.
summary.one_liner: A semi-mechanistic ODE model of zebrafish maternal-to-zygotic transition is fitted to time-course RNA-seq data, and its inferred parameters are used with fuzzy c-means clustering to group genes by shared expression baselines, compared against a shape-based smooth-trajectory clustering.
summary.plain: Early zebrafish embryos first run on molecules supplied by the egg, then switch to making their own genetic instructions. This paper builds a mathematical model of that handover and fits it to measurements of gene activity in zebrafish from early stages up to 120 hours after fertilization. The authors then group genes by patterns the model predicts, and compare these groups with groups formed from the plain shape of each gene's activity curve.
summary.why: The authors report that grouping genes by model parameters gives clusters linked to the timing of zygotic genome activation, which they describe as more precise than shape-only grouping. The paper also reports that the data carry technical bias from the poly(A) enrichment step, a caveat that matters for anyone interpreting such time-course sequencing data. The text does not say how large or general these gains are.

papers.abstract: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.

papers.title: Mechanical canalization of chiral gut morphogenesis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766015 v1

summary.background:
- Chirality (handedness): an object that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like a left vs. right hand.
- Left-right asymmetry: normally, body organs are patterned to one side by specific genes; here the authors say no known asymmetric gene expression is involved in the gut.
- Myosin 1C: a motor protein that helps cells generate and shape mechanical force.
- Epithelium: a sheet of tightly joined cells that lines organs and tubes.
- Longitudinal muscle: muscle fibers running along the length of the gut, built by migrating cells.
- Buckling instability: the tendency of a stretched tube or rod to bend sideways under compression, like a bent straw pressed at its ends.
- Light-sheet imaging: a microscopy method that illuminates a thin slice of a living sample to image it over time with little damage.
summary.one_liner: In the embryonic Drosophila midgut, handedness is set by Myosin 1C in the neighboring hindgut epithelium, relayed through longitudinal muscle precursors, and then amplified into a stereotyped coil by buckling and confinement during elongation.
summary.plain: Many organs in animal bodies are not symmetrical, and they twist into a consistent left-handed or right-handed shape. This paper studies the fruit fly embryo's gut, which coils into a looped shape with alternating handedness, even though no known left-right genes are switched on in it. The authors used multi-angle microscopy, 3D shape measurements, and physical models to trace the handedness back to a nearby organ, the hindgut, where the protein Myosin 1C is expressed.
summary.why: It shows how a tiny, early bias passed between neighboring tissues can be turned into a reliable large-scale body shape by physical forces alone. The text does not discuss implications beyond fly development, so any link to vertebrate left-right patterning or human organ malformations would be speculative.

papers.abstract: Chiral organs such as the gut develop complex, stereotyped shapes, despite variability in the molecular and cellular processes that build them. How cell activity specifies tissue-scale handedness and reproducibly shapes whole organs remains unclear. Here, we use the embryonic Drosophila midgut to understand how a symmetric tubular organ reliably coils into a complex loop of alternating handedness, without any known left-right asymmetric gene expression.Through multi-view light-sheet imaging, 3D geometric analysis, and physical modeling, we show that midgut handedness is specified by epithelial cells in a neighboring organ, relayed across all three germ layers, and finally amplified and canalized by the mechanics of confined gut elongation. Myosin 1C expression in the hindgut epithelium controls midgut handedness up to hundreds of microns away, transmitting chiral bias to the midgut through migratory cells that form the longitudinal muscle. As the midgut elongates, a buckling instability then amplifies early left-right asymmetric constrictions, and confinement funnels the organ into a stereotyped coil. Tissue mechanics thus canalizes organ shape into one of two chiral forms, selected by an inter-organ cellular relay.

papers.title: STL1267 alters HIF-1α and REV-ERBα localization and transcriptional responses in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767081 v1

summary.background:
- HIF-1α: a protein that accumulates when oxygen is low and switches on genes for adapting to hypoxia.
- CoCl2 (cobalt chloride): a chemical used in labs to mimic low-oxygen conditions.
- REV-ERB (REV-ERBα): a nuclear receptor, a protein that sits in the cell's nucleus and regulates gene activity, including circadian (daily) rhythm and metabolism.
- Agonist: a molecule that activates a receptor; STL1267 is described as a REV-ERB agonist.
- ATF4: a stress-response transcription factor that turns on amino-acid and one-carbon metabolism genes.
- RNA sequencing: a method that measures how active each gene is by counting its RNA messages.
- Immunofluorescence: staining proteins with fluorescent markers to see where they are in cells under a microscope.
- False discovery rate (FDR): a statistical threshold used to limit false positives when testing thousands of genes.
summary.one_liner: In CoCl2-treated HeLa cells, the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 shifted HIF-1α and REV-ERBα protein localization and reshaped hypoxia-linked gene expression, notably inducing an ATF4-associated amino-acid and one-carbon metabolism program.
summary.plain: Cells often respond to low oxygen by switching which genes they use and how they process nutrients. This study used cobalt chloride, a chemical that mimics low oxygen, on cultured cervical cancer cells, and tested a drug-like compound (STL1267) that targets REV-ERB, a protein that helps control daily rhythms and metabolism. The researchers looked at where certain proteins sat inside the cells and measured which genes switched on or off.
summary.why: It suggests a possible link between where regulatory proteins sit inside a cell and how the cell copes with metabolic stress, which could matter for understanding how cells adapt to low oxygen, such as in tumors. The text is a small study in one cell line, so any wider significance is uncertain and would need follow-up work.

papers.abstract: Background: REV-ERB nuclear receptors regulate gene expression and cellular metabolism, but their role in the response to hypoxia-associated stress remains unclear. We examined how the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 affects protein distribution and gene expression in HeLa cells exposed to cobalt chloride (CoCl2). Methods and Results: Immunofluorescence microscopy and RNA sequencing were used to compare vehicle-treated controls, cells exposed to CoCl2 plus vehicle, and cells exposed to CoCl2 plus STL1267. Representative images showed stronger nuclear HIF-1 staining after CoCl2 exposure. Nuclear staining was less pronounced with STL1267, while REV-ERB showed more extranuclear staining. CoCl2 exposure altered 267 genes, and STL1267 treatment during CoCl2 exposure altered 132 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05. STL1267 increased ATF4 expression alongside genes involved in amino-acid synthesis and one-carbon metabolism, including ASNS, PHGDH, PSAT1, PSPH and MTHFD2. CTH and CHAC1 also increased, highlighting changes in sulfur-amino-acid metabolism and glutathione turnover. Among the genes induced by CoCl2, CA9, BNIP3 and LDHA decreased with STL1267, whereas HK2, PDK1 and VEGFA did not change significantly. Conclusions: STL1267 selectively reshapes hypoxia-associated gene expression and induces an ATF4-associated metabolic transcriptional program in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells, alongside qualitative changes in HIF-1 and REV-ERB distribution. These findings identify a potential connection between protein compartmentalization and metabolic stress responses, providing a basis for investigating how REV-ERB ligands influence cellular adaptation to oxygen limitation.

papers.title: Development of synthetic genetic arrays for studying interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766915 v1

summary.background:
- Mitochondria are organelles that produce cellular energy and have their own small genome, separate from the nuclear genome.
- COX2 is a mitochondrial gene that encodes part of a respiratory enzyme; its expression serves as the readout here.
- Yeast is a simple single-celled model organism widely used for genetic screens.
- Genetic interaction: when a mutation in one gene changes the effect of a mutation in another, suggesting the two gene products work together or in related processes.
- Homoplasmy means all copies of mitochondrial DNA in a cell are the same version.
- Biolistic bombardment is a method of firing DNA-coated particles into cells to introduce changes to mitochondrial DNA.
- Temperature-sensitive mutants work normally at one temperature but lose function at a higher one.
- Superfolder GFP is a bright, fast-folding green fluorescent protein used as a reporter of gene activity.
- Rim101 is a yeast signaling pathway that responds to environmental cues such as pH.
summary.one_liner: The authors built a genome-wide yeast library of nuclear gene deletions and temperature-sensitive mutants carrying a superfolder-GFP reporter for mitochondrial COX2 expression, and used it to map nuclear genes that raise or lower mitochondrial gene expression.
summary.plain: Mitochondria are the cell's energy-producing compartments, and they carry a small set of their own genes alongside the many genes stored in the cell nucleus. This paper asks how those two sets of genes talk to each other. The authors used baker's yeast, where they could change the mitochondrial DNA, and tagged a mitochondrial gene (COX2) with a fluorescent glow marker so they could measure its activity across thousands of nuclear gene mutants.
summary.why: The screen points to nuclear processes that were not previously expected to affect mitochondrial gene expression, such as the Rim101 signaling pathway and vesicle trafficking. Because mitochondrial dysfunction is linked to aging and many diseases, a platform like this could help future studies, though the text itself does not show how these links apply outside yeast.

papers.abstract: Mitochondria, the central axis of metabolism and energy transformation has emerged as a focal point for understanding the aging process and a plethora of human diseases. Yet, how the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes communicate is still unclear. This work aims to allow the analysis of such crosstalk by developing a genome-wide platform for studying genetic interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Using yeast as a model system in which mitochondrial homoplasmy and stable alterations in the mitochondrial genome can be generated by biolistic bombardment, we created a genome-wide library of yeast cells carrying nuclear deletions and temperature-sensitive mutations together with a superfolder-GFP reporter for the expression of the mitochondrial-encoded COX2 gene. Using this approach, we found links between nuclear-encoded processes and mitochondrial gene expression not previously anticipated, including a requirement for genes involved in MVB (multivesicular body) sorting/RIM signaling, vesicle trafficking/glycosylation, polarity, and peroxisome biogenesis, for maintaining mitochondrial COX2 expression. In contrast, defects in the autophagy machineries, ribosome biogenesis, and nuclear transcription and chromatin organization resulted in increased expression of COX2. While reduced COX2 expression correlated with a reduced expression of the nuclear-encoded TOM70 gene in mutants defect in mitochondrial functions, expression of the mitochondrial and nuclear genes responded differently to defects in cytoplasmic ribosome biogenesis and autophagy. When creating the COX2 expression library, we also found that cells devoid of mitochondrial DNA rely on the Rim101 signaling pathway, and many of its auxiliary regulatory factors, to maintain fitness. As mutations in the Rim101 signaling pathway also caused down-regulation of COX2 expression, it appears that Rim101 signaling is central for maintaining proper control of mitochondrial function. We believe the approach will allow for future genome-wide studies on how nuclear-encoded processes influence the translation, protein folding, and processing of mitochondria-encoded genes.

papers.title: Alkyladenine DNA glycosylase regulates TDG-mediated demethylation and neuronal gene expression by competitive substrate binding
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766739 v1

summary.background:
- DNA methylation: a chemical tag on DNA (mainly on cytosine) that usually silences genes.
- Active demethylation: removing these tags through oxidized forms (such as 5fC) and repair enzymes, not just by passive dilution.
- DNA glycosylases (TDG, AAG): enzymes that cut out damaged or modified bases as the first step of repair.
- Single-strand break (SSB): a nick in one strand of the DNA backbone, which can be an intermediate of demethylation.
- Neurospheres and induced neurons (iNs): lab-grown clusters of neural cells and neurons made from other cells, used as models of brain development.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing: measuring which genes are active in individual cells.
summary.one_liner: Mouse and human neuronal models show that the glycosylase AAG competes with TDG for oxidized methylcytosine substrates (notably 5fC), and this competition tunes active DNA demethylation, single-strand break formation, and neurodevelopmental gene expression.
summary.plain: Cells sometimes remove chemical tags from their DNA to switch genes on or off, and this process briefly leaves small cuts in the DNA strand. This paper asks whether a second repair enzyme, AAG, takes part in that process during brain cell development, alongside the enzyme TDG. The authors found that losing AAG disturbed the timing of neuron-related gene activity in developing mouse and human neurons, and that AAG and TDG compete for the same DNA targets.
summary.why: It suggests that the balance between two DNA-repair enzymes, rather than one enzyme alone, can set how finely genes are timed during neurodevelopment. The text does not link these findings to any disease, so any clinical relevance is unclear from this work alone.

papers.abstract: Endogenous single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs) that arise during active DNA demethylation, regulate neurodevelopmental gene expression. Thymine (TDG) and alkyladenine (AAG) DNA glycosylases recognize oxidized methylcytosines. While TDG is required for excision, role of AAG in active demethylation and neurodevelopment remains unknown. Using mouse neurospheres, hippocampus, and human induced neurons (iNs), we show that AAG is needed for neurogenesis. Loss of AAG contributes to delayed neurodevelopmental and premature synaptic gene expression, evident from single-cell RNA sequencing of differentiating iNs. Synaptic gene expression is co-regulated by both AAG and TDG, with loss of single glycosylase inducing an opposing effect, implying competition. Single-molecule and biochemical assays directly demonstrate this competition, with AAG inhibiting TDG on 5fC. Without AAG, TDG has higher affinity, resulting in reduced global 5fC and increased SSB intermediates. In summary, AAG substrate competition plays an important role in fine tuning active demethylation, thereby regulating gene expression and DNA breaks during neurogenesis.

papers.title: ORGANOID- BASED ASSESSMENT OF ENHANCER ACTIVITY VIA RECOMBINATION-MEDIATED TRANGENESIS
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766570 v1

summary.background:
- Enhancer: a DNA segment that controls when and where a nearby gene is turned on.
- Cis-regulatory element (CRE): a DNA sequence that regulates genes on the same chromosome; enhancers are one type.
- Transgenesis: inserting an extra piece of engineered DNA into an organism or cell to study it.
- Reporter construct: a DNA piece that makes a visible signal (such as a fluorescent protein) when the enhancer under test is active.
- Copy number and position effects: random insertions can differ in how many copies they add and where they land, which can distort results.
- PhiC31 recombinase: an enzyme that inserts DNA at a defined site in the genome, allowing controlled single-copy insertion.
- iPS cells: adult cells reprogrammed into stem cells that can become many cell types.
- Organoid: a small 3D tissue culture grown from stem cells, here modeling parts of the developing brain.
- FOXG1 and POU3F2: transcription factor genes important in brain development.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces RepoV, a PhiC31-mediated transgenesis vector that places single-copy enhancer reporters into human iPS cells, which are then used to test candidate neurodevelopmental enhancers (including POU3F2 and FOXG1 elements) in neural organoids.
summary.plain: Genes are switched on and off by short stretches of DNA called enhancers, and many disease-linked changes in human DNA sit in these regions. This paper describes a way to test such stretches in human stem cells that are grown into small brain-like tissue clumps (organoids), rather than only in mice or zebrafish. The authors report that the method reproduced the activity of enhancers already known to work, and that two FOXG1 enhancers behaved differently in zebrafish than in human organoids, with the organoid results matching the gene's real expression pattern and patient-linked findings.
summary.why: Many human genetic variants found in patients fall outside genes, and it is hard to tell whether they matter. A human-cell test that controls for how many copies of a construct are inserted and where it lands could make such tests more reliable. The text does not report the size of the study or statistical strength, so its general usefulness remains to be seen in wider testing.

papers.abstract: Functional characterization of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) is essential for understanding developmental gene regulation and interpreting human noncoding variation. However, conventional transgenesis assays are limited by integration copy number variability and genomic position effects, while species-specific developmental differences constrain the study of human regulatory sequences in classical model organisms, demanding assays based on human-specific contexts. Here, we developed RepoV, a transgenesis vector enabling single-copy integration of enhancer reporter constructs in the genome of human iPS cells through PhiC31-mediated recombination. Transgenic iPSCs were subsequently used to assess candidate neurodevelopmental enhancers in neural organoids. RepoV recapitulated the expected activity of previously characterized regulatory elements and enabled the evaluation of candidate sequences associated with the neurodevelopmental genes POU3F2 and FOXG1. Notably, two FOXG1 enhancers displayed different activities in zebrafish larvae and human neural organoids. The organoid results were more consistent with endogenous the FOXG1 expression and the pathological phenotypes associated with disease-related regulatory variants identified in patients. Together, these findings establish RepoV transgenesis combined with human organoid cultures as a valuable platform for the functional evaluation of human developmental regulatory sequences.

papers.title: Force regulates mitotic entry timing during Drosophila gastrulation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766297 v1

summary.background:
- Gastrulation: the early embryo stage when a flat layer of cells folds and rearranges to form internal tissues.
- Mesoderm invagination: the inward folding of a group of cells (mesoderm) that drives this shape change.
- Mitotic entry: the point at which a cell commits to dividing, controlled by biochemical regulators of the cell cycle.
- Mitotic domains: stereotyped patches of cells across the embryo that enter division in a coordinated pattern.
- Adherens junctions: protein connections between neighbouring cells that transmit pulling forces across the tissue.
- Contractility: the ability of cells to pull on their neighbours via internal molecular motors.
summary.one_liner: In Drosophila gastrulation, the authors test whether tissue-scale mechanical forces from mesoderm invagination and adherens-junction-dependent force transmission influence the timing of mitotic entry in stereotyped mitotic domains, with a suggested role for mesoderm invagination in mitotic domain 1 timing.
summary.plain: Early in fruit fly development, a sheet of cells folds inward and, at the same time, groups of cells in set regions start dividing. This short text asks whether the physical pulling and folding forces of that movement help set when those cells enter division. The authors disrupted the cell junctions that transmit force across the embryo, and examined mutants that fail to fold the mesoderm, then looked at when cells entered division; they report that the folding appears to matter for timing in one region.
summary.why: It asks whether mechanical forces, not only chemical signals, can set when cells divide during tissue shaping, a question relevant to how development stays coordinated. The text is only an abstract-level summary, so the strength of the link is not clear from it alone.

papers.abstract: Cell division and cell shape changes drive tissue morphogenesis. Cell division is tightly regulated by biochemical factors that influence the cell cycle. Past work in our lab showed how contractility of mesoderm cells influences cell division orientation during Drosophila gastrulation. Whether contractile forces that drive morphogenetic folding influence the timing of coincident mitotic divisions is unknown. During Drosophila gastrulation, cell division is regulated by mitotic entry of cells in stereotypic regions across the embryo, termed mitotic domains. Here, we examine the role of morphogenesis in the timing of mitotic entry in the mitotic domains. To do this, we disrupted adherens junctions to globally disrupt force transmission across the embryo. In addition, we examined the timing of mitotic entry in mutants that affect mesoderm invagination. Our data suggests a role for mesoderm invagination in mitotic domain 1 timing.

papers.title: Accessibility-guided targeting of NRF2-responsive long noncoding RNA NMRAL2P alters a distinct gene expression program and reduces non-small cell lung cancer proliferation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.765723 v1

summary.background:
- NRF2 is a transcription factor: a protein that switches genes on, mainly genes for antioxidant and detoxifying defenses.
- Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer.
- Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) is an RNA molecule that is not translated into protein but can regulate other genes.
- A pseudogene is a once-functional gene copy that has lost its ability to make protein; this one is derived from such a copy.
- SHAPE-MaP is a chemical probing method that shows which parts of an RNA are folded or exposed, so researchers can pick accessible sites to target.
- Antisense gapmers are short synthetic DNA-like strands that bind a target RNA and cause its breakdown.
- MAPK signaling is a cell pathway relaying growth and stress signals; cell adhesion refers to how cells attach to each other and their surroundings.
- Cisplatin is a chemotherapy drug that damages DNA.
summary.one_liner: In lung cancer cells, the stress-response factor NRF2 drives expression of the nuclear pseudogene-derived lncRNA NMRAL2P, whose knockdown with SHAPE-MaP-guided antisense gapmers reduces proliferation, increases cisplatin sensitivity, and alters a restricted cell adhesion and MAPK gene program distinct from NRF2 loss.
summary.plain: Lung cancers that are overactive in a cell-protection pathway (NRF2) help tumor cells survive and resist treatment, but the full set of molecules they rely on is not well mapped. This paper studies a non-coding RNA, NMRAL2P, that NRF2 switches on and that stays in the cell nucleus. Reducing its levels with designed antisense molecules slowed lung cancer cell growth and made cells more sensitive to cisplatin, a chemotherapy drug.
summary.why: It suggests a possible target downstream of NRF2 that works beyond the well-known antioxidant role, which matters because NRF2-active tumors are hard to treat. The mechanism linking this RNA to cell adhesion and MAPK signaling is not yet worked out, so the link to a therapy is still speculative.

papers.abstract: Aberrant activation of the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 promotes non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) survival and therapy resistance, but downstream effectors beyond redox regulation remain incompletely defined. Transcriptome profiling of lung and NSCLC cells identified the pseudogene-derived long noncoding RNA LOC344887/NMRAL2P as consistently associated with NRF2 activity. The NMRAL2P locus produces three predominant, nuclear-localized isoforms whose expression depends on NRF2 across normal lung, lung adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous carcinoma cells. In-cell SHAPE-MaP identified accessible regions within NMRAL2P transcripts, guiding antisense gapmer design. NMRAL2P depletion inhibited NSCLC cell proliferation and increased sensitivity to cisplatin. Transcriptome analysis revealed that NMRAL2P depletion altered a restricted gene expression program involving cell adhesion and MAPK signaling, with responses distinct from those observed following NRF2 depletion. Core NRF2 antioxidant target genes were largely unaffected by NMRAL2P depletion. These findings support a model in which NRF2 induces NMRAL2P to sustain a distinct gene expression program that contributes to NSCLC proliferation and survival. NMRAL2P represents an RNA effector downstream of NRF2 that links oncogenic NRF2 activity to cellular functions beyond canonical antioxidant responses, providing a potential point of intervention in NRF2-active lung cancers and motivating further investigation of the mechanisms connecting this nuclear RNA to signaling pathways.
